metadata.title: Why a Glowing PET Scan Doesn't Actually Show Cancer

metadata.note: Card exclusions honored: NO five-modality tour, NO biodistribution decision tree, NO activatable probes, NO anatomical/molecular hierarchy section. Keep: signal = metabolism proxy, so false positives (inflammation, brown fat, healing wounds) and false negatives (low-glycolytic tumors) happen. Illustrative example: 58-year-old, three reactive lymph nodes after breast cancer surgery, all three high FDG uptake from URI — no malignant cells on biopsy.

props.command: Why a Glowing PET Scan Doesn't Actually Show Cancer?

beats.narration_text: This is Liam, in for Bear. Three lymph nodes, lighting up bright on the PET scan. A surgical team moves to plan salvage radiation. The scan is technically correct. The diagnosis is completely wrong.

items.label: Bright nodes on PET
items.sub: Three lymph nodes, lighting up

items.label: Plan salvage radiation
items.sub: Surgical team moves on the scan

items.label: Diagnosis: wrong
items.sub: Scan technically correct — reading is not

beats.narration_text: FDG-PET is the standard tool for staging cancer and checking for recurrence. Bright spots on the scan mean the tracer has accumulated. Surgeons and oncologists act on those bright spots every day.

items.label: Standard for staging
items.sub: Also used to check for recurrence

items.label: Bright = tracer trapped
items.sub: Radiotracer accumulates in bright pixels

items.label: Clinicians act on it
items.sub: Surgeons and oncologists — every day

beats.narration_text: A PET scan is used to detect cancer. The tracer isn't looking for cancer cells. What is it actually measuring — and when does that difference matter?

lines: A PET scan is used to detect cancer.
The tracer isn't looking for cancer cells.
What is it actually measuring — and when does the gap matter?

beats.narration_text: FDG stands for fluorodeoxyglucose — a radioactive version of glucose. Cells take it up through the same transporters they use for sugar, and trap it inside. The camera counts where the decay happens.

props.title: How FDG gets trapped in a cell

items.label: Enters like glucose
items.sub: Same transporters cells use for sugar

items.label: Trapped inside
items.sub: Cell phosphorylates it — cannot leave

items.label: Camera counts decay
items.sub: Bright pixel = radioactive tally point

beats.narration_text: The PET camera doesn't see cancer. It sees glucose metabolism — specifically, hexokinase activity and glucose-transporter expression. Tumors glow because they burn glucose fast. The Warburg effect: cancer cells favor glycolysis even when oxygen is available.

items.label: Hexokinase activity
items.sub: The enzyme that traps FDG

items.label: Glucose transporters
items.sub: The cell's sugar-import channels

items.label: The Warburg effect
items.sub: Cancer favors glycolysis — even with oxygen

beats.narration_text: And glucose metabolism is not unique to cancer. Activated immune cells in an infection light up just as bright. A healing surgical site glows for weeks. Brown adipose tissue — cold-activated fat in the neck and chest — fires like a lymph node.

props.title: Other things that burn glucose fast

items.label: Infection
items.sub: Activated immune cells — bright as tumor

items.label: Healing wound
items.sub: A surgical site glows for weeks

items.label: Brown fat
items.sub: Cold-activated in neck and chest

beats.narration_text: False negatives are equally real. Tumors with low glycolytic flux — well-differentiated thyroid cancers, some prostate cancers, mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas — may take up almost no FDG despite substantial tumor burden. A dark scan is not an empty scan.

items.label: Well-differentiated thyroid
items.sub: Low glycolytic flux — FDG barely trapped

items.label: Some prostate cancers
items.sub: Substantial burden, dark on FDG

items.label: Mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas
items.sub: A dark scan is not an empty scan

beats.narration_text: Every imaging signal is a proxy. It reports what the tumor tends to do — not the tumor itself. That's why every clinical imaging report says 'consistent with' or 'suspicious for', never 'confirms'. Imaging suggests. Biopsy confirms.

lines: Every imaging signal is a proxy.

beats.narration_text: Here's an illustrative case. A 58-year-old patient — breast cancer surgery three months prior. FDG-PET for recurrence surveillance. Three lymph nodes light up in the chest, each with high uptake. The team flags them for salvage radiation.

items.label: 58, three months post-op
items.sub: Breast cancer surgery, now on surveillance

items.label: Three chest nodes light up
items.sub: Each with high FDG uptake

items.label: Team flags for radiation
items.sub: Salvage plan built on the scan

beats.narration_text: On biopsy: all three are reactive lymph nodes. The patient had a mild upper-respiratory infection the week before the scan. No malignant cells in any of them. The scan was technically correct — it found high glucose metabolism. It just found the wrong cause. Numbers are illustrative.

items.label: All three: reactive
items.sub: No malignant cells in any node

items.label: Mild URI the week before
items.sub: Immune cells lit the nodes up

items.label: Right signal, wrong cause
items.sub: PET saw metabolism — read it as tumor

beats.narration_text: The PET scan did its job. It faithfully reported elevated glucose metabolism in three lymph nodes. The error wasn't the scanner. It was the assumption that high metabolism means cancer.

lines: High glucose metabolism is not cancer.

beats.narration_text: FDG-PET doesn't show cancer. It shows glucose metabolism — and cancer is one of many things that raise it. Every imaging signal is a proxy: it reports what tissue tends to do, not what it is. That's why imaging suggests and biopsy confirms.

lines: FDG-PET shows glucose metabolism, not cancer.
Every imaging signal is a proxy — a shadow of the biology.

beats.narration_text: The verdict. FDG-PET counts where glucose is being burned — not where cancer is. Inflammation, healing wounds, brown fat, and activated immune cells all light up the same way. Low-glycolytic tumors — well-differentiated thyroid, some prostate, mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas — can hide in a dark scan. The scanner is right. The causal jump is wrong. Imaging suggests. Biopsy confirms.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take a diagnostic tool you rely on — a benchmark, an eval, a metric. Name the proxy it actually measures. List three real-world causes that could push it up when the underlying thing hasn't moved, and one condition where the underlying thing has moved but the proxy stays dark. That gap is your imaging-suggests-biopsy-confirms line.
